claim: Mice with chronic constriction injury (CCI) of the left sciatic nerve showed hypersensitivity reflected in the decrease of mechanical pain thresholds measured in the ipsilateral hind paw after 16 days.
source: Mice with chronic constriction injury (CCI) of the left sciatic nerve showed the expected hypersensitivity reflected in the decrease of mechanical pain thresholds measured in the ipsilateral hind paw after 16 days (Figure 1a and b).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements of mechanical pain thresholds in CCI mice shown in Figure 1b.

claim: mGlu5-mediated PI hydrolysis was amplified in the contralateral infralimbic cortex of CCI mice compared to sham-operated mice.
source: mGlu5-mediated PI hydrolysis (i.e. the extent of VU0360172-stimulated InsP formation) was amplified in the contralateral infralimbic cortex, prelimbic cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, and basolateral amygdala (BLA), but not in the contralateral ventrobasal thalamus (VPL), of CCI mice compared to the corresponding regions of sham-operated mice (Figure 1c–g).
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements of InsP levels after VU0360172 stimulation shown in Figure 1c.

claim: mGlu5-mediated PI hydrolysis was amplified in the contralateral prelimbic cortex of CCI mice compared to sham-operated mice.
source: mGlu5-mediated PI hydrolysis (i.e. the extent of VU0360172-stimulated InsP formation) was amplified in the contralateral infralimbic cortex, prelimbic cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, and basolateral amygdala (BLA), but not in the contralateral ventrobasal thalamus (VPL), of CCI mice compared to the corresponding regions of sham-operated mice (Figure 1c–g).
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements of InsP levels after VU0360172 stimulation shown in Figure 1d.

claim: mGlu5-mediated PI hydrolysis was amplified in the contralateral anterior cingulate cortex of CCI mice compared to sham-operated mice.
source: mGlu5-mediated PI hydrolysis (i.e. the extent of VU0360172-stimulated InsP formation) was amplified in the contralateral infralimbic cortex, prelimbic cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, and basolateral amygdala (BLA), but not in the contralateral ventrobasal thalamus (VPL), of CCI mice compared to the corresponding regions of sham-operated mice (Figure 1c–g).
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements of InsP levels after VU0360172 stimulation shown in Figure 1e.

claim: mGlu5-mediated PI hydrolysis was amplified in the contralateral basolateral amygdala of CCI mice compared to sham-operated mice.
source: mGlu5-mediated PI hydrolysis (i.e. the extent of VU0360172-stimulated InsP formation) was amplified in the contralateral infralimbic cortex, prelimbic cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, and basolateral amygdala (BLA), but not in the contralateral ventrobasal thalamus (VPL), of CCI mice compared to the corresponding regions of sham-operated mice (Figure 1c–g).
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements of InsP levels after VU0360172 stimulation shown in Figure 1f.

claim: mGlu5-mediated PI hydrolysis was not amplified in the contralateral ventrobasal thalamus of CCI mice compared to sham-operated mice.
source: mGlu5-mediated PI hydrolysis (i.e. the extent of VU0360172-stimulated InsP formation) was amplified in the contralateral infralimbic cortex, prelimbic cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, and basolateral amygdala (BLA), but not in the contralateral ventrobasal thalamus (VPL), of CCI mice compared to the corresponding regions of sham-operated mice (Figure 1c–g).
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements of InsP levels after VU0360172 stimulation shown in Figure 1g.

claim: mGlu5 receptor protein levels were up-regulated in the contralateral infralimbic cortex of CCI mice.
source: mGlu5 receptor protein levels were up-regulated in the contralateral infralimbic cortex, but not in other brain regions, of CCI mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: mGlu5 receptor protein levels were not up-regulated in the contralateral prelimbic cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, amygdala, or thalamus of CCI mice.
source: mGlu5 receptor protein levels were up-regulated in the contralateral infralimbic cortex, but not in other brain regions, of CCI mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b-e.

claim: mGlu5 receptors become hyperactive in at least four regions of the pain matrix after induction of neuropathic pain.
source: The findings suggest that mGlu5 receptors become hyperactive at least in four regions of the pain matrix after induction of neuropathic pain.
evidence: Inferred from the amplified mGlu5-mediated PI hydrolysis data in infralimbic cortex, prelimbic cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, and basolateral amygdala.

claim: Light-induced activation of JF-NP-26 in the infralimbic cortex contralateral to CCI caused rapid and robust antinociception in neuropathic mice.
source: Light-induced activation of JF-NP-26 in the infralimbic cortex, prelimbic cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, or thalamus (VPL) contralateral to CCI caused rapid and robust antinociception in neuropathic mice measured as increased mechanical thresholds, whereas, unexpectedly, JF-NP-26 activation in the amygdala (BLA) further reduced mechanical pain thresholds, indicating pronociceptive effects (Figure 2d–h).
evidence: Supported by behavioral measurements of mechanical thresholds shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Light-induced activation of JF-NP-26 in the prelimbic cortex contralateral to CCI caused rapid and robust antinociception in neuropathic mice.
source: Light-induced activation of JF-NP-26 in the infralimbic cortex, prelimbic cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, or thalamus (VPL) contralateral to CCI caused rapid and robust antinociception in neuropathic mice measured as increased mechanical thresholds, whereas, unexpectedly, JF-NP-26 activation in the amygdala (BLA) further reduced mechanical pain thresholds, indicating pronociceptive effects (Figure 2d–h).
evidence: Supported by behavioral measurements of mechanical thresholds shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Light-induced activation of JF-NP-26 in the anterior cingulate cortex contralateral to CCI caused rapid and robust antinociception in neuropathic mice.
source: Light-induced activation of JF-NP-26 in the infralimbic cortex, prelimbic cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, or thalamus (VPL) contralateral to CCI caused rapid and robust antinociception in neuropathic mice measured as increased mechanical thresholds, whereas, unexpectedly, JF-NP-26 activation in the amygdala (BLA) further reduced mechanical pain thresholds, indicating pronociceptive effects (Figure 2d–h).
evidence: Supported by behavioral measurements of mechanical thresholds shown in Figure 2f.

claim: Light-induced activation of JF-NP-26 in the thalamus contralateral to CCI caused rapid and robust antinociception in neuropathic mice.
source: Light-induced activation of JF-NP-26 in the infralimbic cortex, prelimbic cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, or thalamus (VPL) contralateral to CCI caused rapid and robust antinociception in neuropathic mice measured as increased mechanical thresholds, whereas, unexpectedly, JF-NP-26 activation in the amygdala (BLA) further reduced mechanical pain thresholds, indicating pronociceptive effects (Figure 2d–h).
evidence: Supported by behavioral measurements of mechanical thresholds shown in Figure 2g.

claim: Light-induced activation of JF-NP-26 in the amygdala contralateral to CCI reduced mechanical pain thresholds, indicating pronociceptive effects.
source: Light-induced activation of JF-NP-26 in the infralimbic cortex, prelimbic cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, or thalamus (VPL) contralateral to CCI caused rapid and robust antinociception in neuropathic mice measured as increased mechanical thresholds, whereas, unexpectedly, JF-NP-26 activation in the amygdala (BLA) further reduced mechanical pain thresholds, indicating pronociceptive effects (Figure 2d–h).
evidence: Supported by behavioral measurements of mechanical thresholds shown in Figure 2h.

claim: Light-induced activation of JF-NP-26 in the prelimbic cortex contralateral to CCI enhanced the mechanical pain threshold in the uninjured hind limb.
source: Interestingly, light-induced activation of JF-NP-26 in the prelimbic cortex contralateral to CCI also enhanced the mechanical pain threshold in the uninjured hind limb (ipsilateral to light delivery), whereas hyperalgesia of the uninjured limb was induced by JF-NP-26 activation in the BLA contralateral to CCI (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by behavioral measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Hyperalgesia of the uninjured limb was induced by JF-NP-26 activation in the BLA contralateral to CCI.
source: Interestingly, light-induced activation of JF-NP-26 in the prelimbic cortex contralateral to CCI also enhanced the mechanical pain threshold in the uninjured hind limb (ipsilateral to light delivery), whereas hyperalgesia of the uninjured limb was induced by JF-NP-26 activation in the BLA contralateral to CCI (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by behavioral measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1d.

claim: No changes in mechanical thresholds were induced by the activation of JF-NP-26 in any brain region of sham-operated mice.
source: No changes in mechanical thresholds were induced by the activation of JF-NP-26 in any brain region of sham-operated mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by behavioral measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: mGlu5 receptor blockade in medial prefrontal cortical regions or thalamus, but not amygdala, is sufficient for antinociceptive effects in neuropathic pain.
source: The data suggest that mGlu5 receptor blockade in medial prefrontal cortical regions (infralimbic, prelimbic, or anterior cingulate cortices) or thalamus, but not amygdala, is sufficient for antinociceptive effects in neuropathic pain.
evidence: Inferred from the behavioral effects of JF-NP-26 activation in different brain regions.

claim: Light-induced activation of JF-NP-26 in the BLA decreased risk-taking behavior in CCI mice.
source: Light-induced activation of JF-NP-26 decreased risk-taking hence increased anxiety-like behavior in CCI mice as shown by the decreased number of entries into, and reduced time spent in, the light compartment of the light-dark box (Figure 2—figure supplement 3a–c).
evidence: Supported by behavioral measurements in the light-dark box test shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3a-c.

claim: Depression-like behavior was unchanged in CCI mice after light-induced irradiation of JF-NP-26 in the BLA.
source: Depression-like behavior assessed with the tail-suspension test was unchanged in CCI mice after light-induced irradiation of JF-NP-26 in the BLA (Figure 2—figure supplement 3d).
evidence: Supported by behavioral measurements in the tail suspension test shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3d.

claim: Systemic injection of alloswitch-1 increased mechanical pain thresholds of CCI mice, indicating antinociceptive effects.
source: Systemic injection of alloswitch-1 (10 mg/kg, i.p.) consistently increased mechanical pain thresholds of CCI mice, indicating antinociceptive effects.
evidence: Supported by behavioral measurements shown in Figure 2j-n.

claim: Blue-violet-light-induced inactivation of alloswitch-1 in the contralateral infralimbic cortex abolished alloswitch-1-induced antinociception.
source: Blue-violet-light-induced inactivation of alloswitch-1 in the contralateral infralimbic cortex, prelimbic cortex, and thalamus (VPL) abolished alloswitch-1-induced antinociception, which was restored by green-light induced reactivation of alloswitch-1 (Figure 2j, k and n).
evidence: Supported by behavioral measurements shown in Figure 2j.

claim: Blue-violet-light-induced inactivation of alloswitch-1 in the contralateral prelimbic cortex abolished alloswitch-1-induced antinociception.
source: Blue-violet-light-induced inactivation of alloswitch-1 in the contralateral infralimbic cortex, prelimbic cortex, and thalamus (VPL) abolished alloswitch-1-induced antinociception, which was restored by green-light induced reactivation of alloswitch-1 (Figure 2j, k and n).
evidence: Supported by behavioral measurements shown in Figure 2k.

claim: Blue-violet-light-induced inactivation of alloswitch-1 in the contralateral thalamus abolished alloswitch-1-induced antinociception.
source: Blue-violet-light-induced inactivation of alloswitch-1 in the contralateral infralimbic cortex, prelimbic cortex, and thalamus (VPL) abolished alloswitch-1-induced antinociception, which was restored by green-light induced reactivation of alloswitch-1 (Figure 2j, k and n).
evidence: Supported by behavioral measurements shown in Figure 2n.

claim: Green-light induced reactivation of alloswitch-1 restored antinociception after blue-violet-light-induced inactivation in the infralimbic cortex, prelimbic cortex, and thalamus.
source: Blue-violet-light-induced inactivation of alloswitch-1 in the contralateral infralimbic cortex, prelimbic cortex, and thalamus (VPL) abolished alloswitch-1-induced antinociception, which was restored by green-light induced reactivation of alloswitch-1 (Figure 2j, k and n).
evidence: Supported by behavioral measurements shown in Figure 2j, k, and n.

claim: Optical inactivation of alloswitch-1 in the amygdala further increased the antinociceptive effects of systemic alloswitch-1.
source: In contrast, optical inactivation of alloswitch-1 in the amygdala (BLA) further increased the antinociceptive effects of systemic alloswitch-1, and this effect was reversed by reactivation of alloswitch-1 (Figure 2m).
evidence: Supported by behavioral measurements shown in Figure 2m.

claim: Reactivation of alloswitch-1 in the amygdala reversed the enhanced antinociception caused by optical inactivation.
source: In contrast, optical inactivation of alloswitch-1 in the amygdala (BLA) further increased the antinociceptive effects of systemic alloswitch-1, and this effect was reversed by reactivation of alloswitch-1 (Figure 2m).
evidence: Supported by behavioral measurements shown in Figure 2m.

claim: Optical modulation of alloswitch-1 in the anterior cingulate cortex had no effect on pain thresholds.
source: Optical modulation of alloswitch-1 in the anterior cingulate cortex had no effect on pain thresholds (Figure 2l).
evidence: Supported by behavioral measurements shown in Figure 2l.

claim: mGlu5 receptor blockade in infralimbic and prelimbic cortices and thalamus, but not anterior cingulate cortex, is necessary for antinociceptive effects in neuropathic pain conditions.
source: The data suggest that mGlu5 receptor blockade in infralimbic and prelimbic cortices and thalamus, but not anterior cingulate cortex, is necessary for antinociceptive effects in neuropathic pain conditions, whereas mGlu5 blockade in the BLA has paradoxical pain-facilitating effects.
evidence: Inferred from the behavioral effects of alloswitch-1 inactivation in different brain regions.

claim: mGlu5 blockade in the BLA has paradoxical pain-facilitating effects.
source: The data suggest that mGlu5 receptor blockade in infralimbic and prelimbic cortices and thalamus, but not anterior cingulate cortex, is necessary for antinociceptive effects in neuropathic pain conditions, whereas mGlu5 blockade in the BLA has paradoxical pain-facilitating effects.
evidence: Inferred from the behavioral effects showing that mGlu5 blockade in BLA reduces pain thresholds.

claim: Alloswitch-1 increased EPSCs in prelimbic pyramidal neurons compared to predrug ACSF values.
source: Administration of mGlu5 NAM alloswitch-1 (100 nM) increased EPSCs compared to predrug ACSF values.
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recordings shown in Figure 3f.

claim: Alloswitch-1 inactivation with blue-violet light slightly decreased EPSCs so that they were not significantly different from baseline values.
source: Alloswitch-1 inactivation with blue-violet light (5 min, 0.5 Hz, 500 ms) slightly decreased EPSCs so that they were not significantly different from baseline values.
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recordings shown in Figure 3f.

claim: Reactivation of alloswitch-1 with green light led to a significant increase in EPSCs compared to predrug.
source: Reactivation of alloswitch-1 with green light (5 min, 0.5 Hz, 500 ms) led to a significant increase in EPSCs compared to predrug (Figure 3d and f).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recordings shown in Figure 3f.

claim: No significant effects were observed on IPSCs in prelimbic pyramidal neurons during alloswitch-1 application and optical modulation.
source: No significant effects were observed on IPSCs (Figure 3e and g).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recordings shown in Figure 3g.

claim: The E/I ratio in prelimbic pyramidal neurons showed increases by alloswitch-1 and by reactivation with green light, and no change from baseline during blue-violet light application.
source: As a result, the E/I ratio showed a pattern that reflected the changes in EPSCs with increases by alloswitch-1 and by reactivation with green light, and no change from baseline during blue-violet light application to inactivate alloswitch-1 (Figure 3h).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recordings shown in Figure 3h.

claim: mGlu5 receptor controls the excitatory drive of prelimbic output neurons, possibly by activation of synaptic inhibition of excitatory inputs.
source: These results suggest that mGlu5 receptor controls the excitatory drive of prelimbic output neurons, possibly by activation of synaptic inhibition of excitatory inputs; and mGlu5 receptor inhibition restores the excitatory drive-in neuropathic pain.
evidence: Inferred from the electrophysiological data showing that mGlu5 NAM increases EPSCs.

claim: mGlu5 receptor inhibition restores the excitatory drive in neuropathic pain.
source: These results suggest that mGlu5 receptor controls the excitatory drive of prelimbic output neurons, possibly by activation of synaptic inhibition of excitatory inputs; and mGlu5 receptor inhibition restores the excitatory drive-in neuropathic pain.
evidence: Inferred from the electrophysiological data showing that mGlu5 NAM increases EPSCs in neuropathic pain conditions.

claim: Systemic administration of alloswitch-1 caused a trend towards decreased excitation of RVM ON cells.
source: Systemic administration of alloswitch-1 (10 mg/kg, i.p.) caused a trend towards decreased excitation of ON cells.
evidence: Supported by in vivo single-unit recordings shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Optical inactivation of alloswitch-1 in the prelimbic cortex increased ON-cell excitation.
source: Optical inactivation of alloswitch-1 in the prelimbic cortex increased ON-cell excitation whereas reactivation of alloswitch-1 with green light decreased excitation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by in vivo single-unit recordings shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Reactivation of alloswitch-1 with green light in the prelimbic cortex decreased ON-cell excitation.
source: Optical inactivation of alloswitch-1 in the prelimbic cortex increased ON-cell excitation whereas reactivation of alloswitch-1 with green light decreased excitation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by in vivo single-unit recordings shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Increased prelimbic cortical output with mGlu receptor inhibition can decrease excitation of pronociceptive RVM ON-cells resulting in antinociceptive behavioral effects.
source: These results suggest that increased prelimbic cortical output with mGlu receptor inhibition (brain slice physiology data) can decrease excitation of pronociceptive RVM ON-cells resulting in antinociceptive behavioral effects (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Inferred from the combination of brain slice physiology and in vivo RVM recordings.

claim: Prefrontal cortical-RVM connectivity is important in mediating the pain-relieving effects associated with mGlu5 receptor inhibition in the prelimbic cortex.
source: These findings highlight the importance of prefrontal cortical-RVM connectivity in mediating the pain-relieving effects associated with mGlu5 receptor inhibition in the prelimbic cortex.
evidence: Inferred from the electrophysiological and behavioral data showing that mGlu5 inhibition in prelimbic cortex affects RVM ON-cells and produces analgesia.

claim: Systemically applied alloswitch-1 increased neuronal activity in prelimbic pyramidal neurons.
source: Systemically applied alloswitch-1 (10 mg/kg, i.p.) increased neuronal activity, but inactivation of alloswitch-1 with blue-violet light illumination in the BLA had no significant effect, arguing against a contribution of mGlu5 in the BLA.
evidence: Supported by in vivo electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1e.

claim: Inactivation of alloswitch-1 with blue-violet light illumination in the BLA had no significant effect on prelimbic neuronal activity.
source: Systemically applied alloswitch-1 (10 mg/kg, i.p.) increased neuronal activity, but inactivation of alloswitch-1 with blue-violet light illumination in the BLA had no significant effect, arguing against a contribution of mGlu5 in the BLA.
evidence: Supported by in vivo electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1e.

claim: Reactivation of alloswitch-1 with green light illumination in the BLA did not mimic the effect of systemic alloswitch-1 on prelimbic neuronal activity.
source: Furthermore, reactivation of alloswitch-1 with green light illumination in the BLA did not mimic the effect of systemic alloswitch-1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by in vivo electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1e.

claim: Alloswitch-1 had significant inhibitory effects on IPSCs at the BLA-CeLC synapse.
source: Alloswitch-1 (100 nM) had significant inhibitory effects on IPSCs at the BLA-CeLC synapse (Figure 3l and n), which was reversed by inactivation with blue-violet light (5 min, 0.5 Hz, 500 ms) so that IPSCs were not significantly different from baseline.
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recordings shown in Figure 3n.

claim: Inactivation of alloswitch-1 with blue-violet light reversed the inhibitory effects on IPSCs at the BLA-CeLC synapse so that IPSCs were not significantly different from baseline.
source: Alloswitch-1 (100 nM) had significant inhibitory effects on IPSCs at the BLA-CeLC synapse (Figure 3l and n), which was reversed by inactivation with blue-violet light (5 min, 0.5 Hz, 500 ms) so that IPSCs were not significantly different from baseline.
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recordings shown in Figure 3n.

claim: Reactivation of alloswitch-1 with green light decreased IPSCs at the BLA-CeLC synapse.
source: Reactivation with green light (5 min, 0.5 Hz, 500 ms) decreased IPSCs.
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recordings shown in Figure 3n.

claim: Alloswitch-1 and its optical modulation had no significant effects on EPSCs at the BLA-CeLC synapse.
source: Alloswitch-1 by itself and its inactivation and reactivation had no significant effects on EPSCs (Figure 3m and o).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recordings shown in Figure 3o.

claim: Alloswitch-1 decreased the inhibition/excitation (I/E) ratio at the BLA-CeLC synapse significantly.
source: Accordingly, alloswitch-1 decreased the inhibition/excitation (I/E) ratio significantly; this effect was reversed with blue-violet light for optical inactivation and was reinstated with green light for reactivation (Figure 3p).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recordings shown in Figure 3p.

claim: The effect of alloswitch-1 on the I/E ratio at the BLA-CeLC synapse was reversed with blue-violet light for optical inactivation.
source: Accordingly, alloswitch-1 decreased the inhibition/excitation (I/E) ratio significantly; this effect was reversed with blue-violet light for optical inactivation and was reinstated with green light for reactivation (Figure 3p).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recordings shown in Figure 3p.

claim: The effect of alloswitch-1 on the I/E ratio at the BLA-CeLC synapse was reinstated with green light for reactivation.
source: Accordingly, alloswitch-1 decreased the inhibition/excitation (I/E) ratio significantly; this effect was reversed with blue-violet light for optical inactivation and was reinstated with green light for reactivation (Figure 3p).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recordings shown in Figure 3p.

claim: mGlu5 blockade reduces BLA-driven feed-forward inhibition onto CeLC neurons.
source: The data suggest that mGlu5 blockade reduces BLA-driven feed-forward inhibition onto CeLC neurons that have been linked mechanistically to pain behaviors, which could explain the hypersensitivity observed with photopharmacological blockade of mGlu5 receptors.
evidence: Inferred from the electrophysiological data showing decreased IPSCs at the BLA-CeLC synapse with mGlu5 NAM.

claim: Reduced BLA-driven feed-forward inhibition onto CeLC neurons could explain the hypersensitivity observed with photopharmacological blockade of mGlu5 receptors.
source: The data suggest that mGlu5 blockade reduces BLA-driven feed-forward inhibition onto CeLC neurons that have been linked mechanistically to pain behaviors, which could explain the hypersensitivity observed with photopharmacological blockade of mGlu5 receptors.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of electrophysiological and behavioral data.

claim: This is the first study to employ photopharmacological tools to compare and contrast distinct roles of mGlu5 receptors in different regions of the pain matrix.
source: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to employ photopharmacological tools to compare and contrast distinct roles of mGlu5 receptors in different regions of the pain matrix.
evidence: Stated by the authors based on their knowledge of the literature.

claim: The net effect of systemic administration of alloswitch-1 was the enhancement of pain thresholds.
source: The net effect of systemic administration of alloswitch-1 was the enhancement of pain thresholds, which is in line with findings obtained with other mGlu5 receptor NAMs in models of neuropathic pain (Lax et al., 2014; Jacob et al., 2009), indicating that the overall effect of the drug across its target regions within the pain neuraxis is the induction of analgesia.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data and consistent with cited literature.

claim: The overall effect of alloswitch-1 across its target regions within the pain neuraxis is the induction of analgesia.
source: The net effect of systemic administration of alloswitch-1 was the enhancement of pain thresholds, which is in line with findings obtained with other mGlu5 receptor NAMs in models of neuropathic pain (Lax et al., 2014; Jacob et al., 2009), indicating that the overall effect of the drug across its target regions within the pain neuraxis is the induction of analgesia.
evidence: Inferred from the behavioral data showing increased pain thresholds with systemic alloswitch-1.

claim: Responses to mGlu5 receptor blockade are not homogenous in different regions of the pain matrix.
source: However, the combined use of mGlu5 NAMs JF-NP-26 (which is activated by blue-violet light) and alloswitch-1 (which is inactivated by blue-violet light and re-activated by green light) showed for the first time that responses to mGlu5 receptor blockade are not homogenous in different regions of the pain matrix.
evidence: Demonstrated by the differential behavioral effects of mGlu5 blockade in different brain regions.

claim: Increases in pain thresholds after local activation of JF-NP-26 in a specific brain region indicate that mGlu5 receptor blockade in that region is sufficient for the induction of analgesia.
source: Increases in pain thresholds after local activation of JF-NP-26 in a specific brain region indicate that mGlu5 receptor blockade in that region is sufficient for the induction of analgesia.
evidence: Logical interpretation of the experimental design and results.

claim: Loss of analgesia after local inactivation of allowitch-1 suggests that mGlu5 receptor blockade in that region is necessary for the overall behavioral effect of a systemic mGlu5 receptor NAM.
source: In contrast, loss of analgesia after local inactivation of allowitch-1 suggests that mGlu5 receptor blockade in that region is necessary for the overall behavioral effect of a systemic mGlu5 receptor NAM.
evidence: Logical interpretation of the experimental design and results.

claim: mGlu5 receptor blockade in the contralateral ventrobasal thalamus and infralimbic and prelimbic subregions of the medial prefrontal cortex was sufficient for the induction of analgesia.
source: We found that mGlu5 receptor blockade in the contralateral ventrobasal thalamus and infralimbic and prelimbic subregions of the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) was sufficient for the induction of analgesia and was also required for the analgesic activity of a systemically administered mGlu5 receptor NAM (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2.

claim: mGlu5 receptor blockade in the contralateral ventrobasal thalamus and infralimbic and prelimbic subregions of the medial prefrontal cortex was required for the analgesic activity of a systemically administered mGlu5 receptor NAM.
source: We found that mGlu5 receptor blockade in the contralateral ventrobasal thalamus and infralimbic and prelimbic subregions of the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) was sufficient for the induction of analgesia and was also required for the analgesic activity of a systemically administered mGlu5 receptor NAM (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Selective optical inactivation of systemic alloswitch-1 in the infralimbic and prelimbic cortices and thalamus blocked the analgesic effect.
source: Conversely, selective optical inactivation of systemic alloswitch-1 in the infralimbic and prelimbic cortices and thalamus blocked the analgesic effect.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2j, k, and n.

claim: Regulation of pain thresholds by mGlu5 receptors in the ventrobasal thalamus and the two more ventral mPFC subregions is not redundant, but rather complementary.
source: These data suggest that regulation of pain thresholds by mGlu5 receptors in the ventrobasal thalamus and the two more ventral mPFC subregions is not redundant, but rather complementary, and that a connection between these three regions is a main target for systemic mGlu5 NAMs in the induction of analgesia in models of neuropathic pain.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that inactivation of alloswitch-1 in any of these regions blocks systemic analgesia.

claim: A connection between the ventrobasal thalamus, infralimbic cortex, and prelimbic cortex is a main target for systemic mGlu5 NAMs in the induction of analgesia in models of neuropathic pain.
source: These data suggest that regulation of pain thresholds by mGlu5 receptors in the ventrobasal thalamus and the two more ventral mPFC subregions is not redundant, but rather complementary, and that a connection between these three regions is a main target for systemic mGlu5 NAMs in the induction of analgesia in models of neuropathic pain.
evidence: Inferred from the photopharmacological data showing the necessity of these regions for systemic analgesia.

claim: Nociceptive sensitization has been consistently associated with hypoactivity of pyramidal neurons in the prelimbic cortex.
source: Nociceptive sensitization has been consistently associated with hypoactivity of pyramidal neurons in the prelimbic cortex, and activation of pyramidal neurons causes analgesia in models of neuropathic pain (Chung et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chung et al., 2018.

claim: Activation of pyramidal neurons in the prelimbic cortex causes analgesia in models of neuropathic pain.
source: Nociceptive sensitization has been consistently associated with hypoactivity of pyramidal neurons in the prelimbic cortex, and activation of pyramidal neurons causes analgesia in models of neuropathic pain (Chung et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chung et al., 2018.

claim: Alloswitch-1 or light-activated JF-NP-26 caused analgesia by antagonizing mGlu5 receptors expressed by inhibitory interneurons, or by excitatory neurons that preferentially activate inhibitory interneurons, within the local circuit.
source: A simplistic hypothesis is that alloswitch-1 or light-activated JF-NP-26 caused analgesia by antagonizing mGlu5 receptors expressed by inhibitory interneurons, or by excitatory neurons that preferentially activate inhibitory interneurons, within the local circuit (Chung et al., 2018).
evidence: Proposed as a hypothesis based on the data and cited literature.

claim: Light-induced inactivation of allowitch-1 in the contralateral anterior cingulate cortex did not abrogate the analgesic activity of the drug.
source: In contrast, light-induced inactivation of allowitch-1 in the contralateral anterior cingulate cortex did not abrogate the analgesic activity of the drug.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2l.

claim: mGlu5 receptor blockade in the anterior cingulate cortex was not necessary for the overall analgesic effect of systemically administered mGlu5 NAM.
source: While mGlu5 receptor blockade in the anterior cingulate cortex was not necessary for the overall analgesic effect of systemically administered mGlu5 NAM, antinociceptive effects of mGlu5 receptor blockade with JF-NP-26 in that region suggest that it plays a significant role in modulating pain behaviors.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that inactivation of alloswitch-1 in anterior cingulate cortex did not block systemic analgesia.

claim: Antinociceptive effects of mGlu5 receptor blockade with JF-NP-26 in the anterior cingulate cortex suggest that it plays a significant role in modulating pain behaviors.
source: While mGlu5 receptor blockade in the anterior cingulate cortex was not necessary for the overall analgesic effect of systemically administered mGlu5 NAM, antinociceptive effects of mGlu5 receptor blockade with JF-NP-26 in that region suggest that it plays a significant role in modulating pain behaviors.
evidence: Inferred from the behavioral data showing that JF-NP-26 activation in anterior cingulate cortex produces analgesia.

claim: There are contrasting reports on the role of mPFC mGlu5 receptors in pain modulation.
source: There are contrasting reports on the role of mPFC mGlu5 receptors in pain modulation (Chung et al., 2018; Kiritoshi et al., 2016; Ji and Neugebauer, 2014; David-Pereira et al., 2016; Palazzo et al., 2014; Giordano et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: The application of mGlu5 receptor antagonists in the ipsilateral prelimbic and infralimbic cortices enhanced neuropathic pain in the spared nerve injury model.
source: For example, the application of mGlu5 receptor antagonists in the ipsilateral prelimbic and infralimbic cortices enhanced neuropathic pain (spared nerve injury) (Giordano et al., 2012), whereas ipsilateral infralimbic application reduced arthritis-induced pain (David-Pereira et al., 2016) and bilateral application in prelimbic cortex caused antinociception in the spinal nerve ligation model of neuropathic pain (Chung et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Giordano et al., 2012.

claim: Ipsilateral infralimbic application of mGlu5 receptor antagonists reduced arthritis-induced pain.
source: For example, the application of mGlu5 receptor antagonists in the ipsilateral prelimbic and infralimbic cortices enhanced neuropathic pain (spared nerve injury) (Giordano et al., 2012), whereas ipsilateral infralimbic application reduced arthritis-induced pain (David-Pereira et al., 2016) and bilateral application in prelimbic cortex caused antinociception in the spinal nerve ligation model of neuropathic pain (Chung et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to David-Pereira et al., 2016.

claim: Bilateral application of mGlu5 receptor antagonists in prelimbic cortex caused antinociception in the spinal nerve ligation model of neuropathic pain.
source: For example, the application of mGlu5 receptor antagonists in the ipsilateral prelimbic and infralimbic cortices enhanced neuropathic pain (spared nerve injury) (Giordano et al., 2012), whereas ipsilateral infralimbic application reduced arthritis-induced pain (David-Pereira et al., 2016) and bilateral application in prelimbic cortex caused antinociception in the spinal nerve ligation model of neuropathic pain (Chung et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chung et al., 2017.

claim: Pharmacological blockade of mGlu5 receptors in the contralateral mPFC caused antinociception in the CCI model of neuropathic pain.
source: Our photopharmacological tools allowed us to establish that pharmacological blockade of mGlu5 receptors in the contralateral mPFC caused antinociception in the CCI model of neuropathic pain, and that prelimbic and infralimbic regions, but not anterior cingulate cortex, play a critical role in mediating systemic mGlu5 NAM antinociception.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data from photopharmacological experiments.

claim: Prelimbic and infralimbic regions, but not anterior cingulate cortex, play a critical role in mediating systemic mGlu5 NAM antinociception.
source: Our photopharmacological tools allowed us to establish that pharmacological blockade of mGlu5 receptors in the contralateral mPFC caused antinociception in the CCI model of neuropathic pain, and that prelimbic and infralimbic regions, but not anterior cingulate cortex, play a critical role in mediating systemic mGlu5 NAM antinociception.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data from photopharmacological experiments.

claim: Previous studies showed increased mGlu5 receptor expression in the mPFC ipsilateral, but not contralateral, to peripheral nerve injury.
source: Previous studies showed increased mGlu5 receptor expression in the mPFC ipsilateral, but not contralateral, to peripheral nerve injury (Chung et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chung et al., 2017.

claim: mGlu5 receptor-mediated PI hydrolysis was significantly amplified in all subregions of the contralateral mPFC and in the contralateral amygdala after induction of neuropathic pain.
source: We found that mGlu5 receptor-mediated PI hydrolysis was significantly amplified in all subregions of the contralateral mPFC and in the contralateral amygdala after induction of neuropathic pain whereas mGlu5 receptor protein levels were significantly increased only in the contralateral infralimbic cortex of neuropathic mice (Figure 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements shown in Figure 1c-f.

claim: In the anterior cingulate cortex, prelimbic cortex, and basolateral amygdala, mGlu5 receptors become hyperactive after the induction of pain.
source: This suggests that, at least in the anterior cingulate cortex, prelimbic cortex, and basolateral amygdala, mGlu5 receptors become hyperactive after the induction of pain.
evidence: Inferred from the amplified PI hydrolysis without corresponding increases in protein levels.

claim: mGlu5 receptor hyperactivity might be mediated by the enhanced coupling of mGlu5 receptors to Gq/11 proteins, increased expression of phospholipase-Cβ, or other mechanisms.
source: It remains to be determined if this is mediated by the enhanced coupling of mGlu5 receptors to Gq/11 proteins, increased expression of phospholipase-Cβ, or other mechanisms.
evidence: Speculative statement about possible mechanisms.

claim: mGlu5 receptor signaling was down-regulated in the thalamus of neuropathic mice.
source: Interestingly, mGlu5 receptor signaling was down-regulated in the thalamus of neuropathic mice, but mGlu5 blockade in the thalamus still had antinociceptive effects (see below).
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements shown in Figure 1g.

claim: mGlu5 blockade in the thalamus had antinociceptive effects despite down-regulated mGlu5 receptor signaling in neuropathic mice.
source: Interestingly, mGlu5 receptor signaling was down-regulated in the thalamus of neuropathic mice, but mGlu5 blockade in the thalamus still had antinociceptive effects (see below).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2g and 2n.

claim: Down-regulation of mGlu5 receptor signaling in the thalamus might represent a compensatory mechanism aimed at mitigating pain in neuropathic mice.
source: Down-regulation of mGlu5 receptor signaling in the thalamus might represent a compensatory mechanism aimed at mitigating pain in neuropathic mice.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: Selective modulation of mGlu5 receptor activity in the infralimbic and prelimbic cortex presents an intriguing opportunity to harness their specific analgesic effects while minimizing potential side effects associated with global mGlu5 receptor blockade.
source: Selective modulation of mGlu5 receptor activity in the infralimbic and prelimbic cortex presents an intriguing opportunity to harness their specific analgesic effects while minimizing potential side effects associated with global mGlu5 receptor blockade.
evidence: Inferred from the findings showing region-specific effects of mGlu5 blockade.

claim: The differential roles of mPFC regions in pain modulation highlight their unique contributions to the complex pain circuitry.
source: The differential roles of mPFC regions in pain modulation highlight their unique contributions to the complex pain circuitry.
evidence: Inferred from the differential behavioral and electrophysiological effects observed in different mPFC subregions.

claim: Targeting the infralimbic and prelimbic cortices allows for a more precise and localized approach, potentially reducing the risk of off-target effects and enhancing the therapeutic efficacy of mGlu5 receptor-based interventions.
source: Targeting the infralimbic and prelimbic cortices allows for a more precise and localized approach, potentially reducing the risk of off-target effects and enhancing the therapeutic efficacy of mGlu5 receptor-based interventions.
evidence: Inferred from the findings showing that these regions are necessary and sufficient for analgesia.

claim: The BLA is a voice out of the chorus in the modulation of pain by mGlu5 receptors in neuropathic mice.
source: Photopharmacology revealed for the first time that the BLA is a voice out of the chorus in the modulation of pain by mGlu5 receptors in neuropathic mice.
evidence: Inferred from the paradoxical pronociceptive effects of mGlu5 blockade in BLA.

claim: mGlu5 receptors in BLA neurons serve antinociceptive functions in neuropathic pain.
source: This suggests that mGlu5 receptors in BLA neurons serve antinociceptive functions in neuropathic pain, and this may limit the overall effect of mGlu5 NAMs in the treatment of pain.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that blocking mGlu5 in BLA produces pronociceptive effects.

claim: mGlu5 receptors in BLA may limit the overall effect of mGlu5 NAMs in the treatment of pain.
source: This suggests that mGlu5 receptors in BLA neurons serve antinociceptive functions in neuropathic pain, and this may limit the overall effect of mGlu5 NAMs in the treatment of pain.
evidence: Inferred from the paradoxical effects of mGlu5 blockade in BLA.

claim: Electrical stimulation of BLA neurons enhanced inhibition of prelimbic neurons.
source: These connections involve direct excitation as well as feedforward inhibition, and previous studies showed that electrical stimulation of BLA neurons enhanced inhibition of prelimbic neurons (Guida et al., 2017; Ishikawa and Nakamura, 2003) and decreased excitation/inhibition balance in pain resulted in impaired mPFC output and behavioral control (Kiritoshi et al., 2016; Cheriyan and Sheets, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Guida et al., 2017 and Ishikawa and Nakamura, 2003.

claim: Decreased excitation/inhibition balance in pain resulted in impaired mPFC output and behavioral control.
source: These connections involve direct excitation as well as feedforward inhibition, and previous studies showed that electrical stimulation of BLA neurons enhanced inhibition of prelimbic neurons (Guida et al., 2017; Ishikawa and Nakamura, 2003) and decreased excitation/inhibition balance in pain resulted in impaired mPFC output and behavioral control (Kiritoshi et al., 2016; Cheriyan and Sheets, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kiritoshi et al., 2016 and Cheriyan and Sheets, 2020.

claim: Impaired feedforward inhibition of CeA output neurons drives pain behaviors.
source: Impaired feedforward inhibition of CeA output neurons drives pain behaviors (Ren et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ren et al., 2013.

claim: Previous studies reported antinociceptive effects of mGlu5 receptor blockade with MPEP in the CeA in inflammatory pain models.
source: Our data suggest pronociceptive effects of mGlu5 NAM in BLA through connections with CeA, whereas previous studies reported antinociceptive effects of mGlu5 receptor blockade with MPEP in the CeA in inflammatory pain models (Han and Neugebauer, 2005; Kolber et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Han and Neugebauer, 2005 and Kolber et al., 2010.

claim: Administration of alloswitch-1 into CeA decreased hypersensitivity in an inflammatory pain model.
source: Administration of alloswitch-1 into CeA also decreased hypersensitivity in an inflammatory pain model (Ricart-Ortega et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ricart-Ortega et al., 2020.

claim: A mGlu5 antagonist (MTEP) inhibited both excitatory and inhibitory transmission in CeA neurons under normal conditions and in an arthritis pain model.
source: Interestingly, a mGlu5 antagonist (MTEP) inhibited both excitatory and inhibitory transmission in CeA neurons under normal conditions and in an arthritis pain model (Ren and Neugebauer, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ren and Neugebauer, 2010.

claim: Differential mGlu5 function in BLA and CeA may serve to shed light onto the intricate amygdala circuitry involved in pain processing and pain modulation.
source: Thus, differential mGlu5 function in BLA and CeA may serve to shed light onto the intricate amygdala circuitry involved in pain processing and pain modulation.
evidence: Inferred from the contrasting effects of mGlu5 blockade in BLA versus CeA.

claim: The application of photopharmacology to the analysis of mGlu5 function in pain discovered novel region-specific differential actions.
source: In summary, the application of photopharmacology to the analysis of mGlu5 function in pain discovered novel region-specific differential actions that need to be considered when targeting these receptors as novel and improved therapeutic targets, and this may have implications for other transmitter and modulator systems.
evidence: Summarizes the main findings of the study.

claim: Novel region-specific differential actions of mGlu5 receptors need to be considered when targeting these receptors as therapeutic targets.
source: In summary, the application of photopharmacology to the analysis of mGlu5 function in pain discovered novel region-specific differential actions that need to be considered when targeting these receptors as novel and improved therapeutic targets, and this may have implications for other transmitter and modulator systems.
evidence: Inferred from the findings showing heterogeneous effects of mGlu5 blockade.

claim: The findings may have implications for other transmitter and modulator systems.
source: In summary, the application of photopharmacology to the analysis of mGlu5 function in pain discovered novel region-specific differential actions that need to be considered when targeting these receptors as novel and improved therapeutic targets, and this may have implications for other transmitter and modulator systems.
evidence: Speculative statement about broader implications.

claim: JF-NP-26 is a caged derivative of the mGlu5 receptor NAM raseglurant, which is inactive on its own and activated by light in the visible spectrum (405 nm).
source: We tested two functionally distinct light-sensitive mGlu5 receptor ligands: (i) a caged derivative of the mGlu5 receptor NAM raseglurant (compound JF-NP-26), which is inactive on its own and activated by light in the visible spectrum (405 nm) Font et al., 2017; and, (ii) the photoswitchable mGlu5 receptor NAM alloswitch-1, which is active on its own, is inactivated by light at 405 nm, and can be re-activated by light at 520 nm (Pittolo et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Font et al., 2017.

claim: Alloswitch-1 is a photoswitchable mGlu5 receptor NAM, which is active on its own, is inactivated by light at 405 nm, and can be re-activated by light at 520 nm.
source: We tested two functionally distinct light-sensitive mGlu5 receptor ligands: (i) a caged derivative of the mGlu5 receptor NAM raseglurant (compound JF-NP-26), which is inactive on its own and activated by light in the visible spectrum (405 nm) Font et al., 2017; and, (ii) the photoswitchable mGlu5 receptor NAM alloswitch-1, which is active on its own, is inactivated by light at 405 nm, and can be re-activated by light at 520 nm (Pittolo et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pittolo et al., 2014.

claim: Light in the visible spectrum does not damage CNS tissue and can be delivered multiple times if needed.
source: In addition, light in the visible spectrum does not damage CNS tissue and can be delivered multiple times if needed.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about visible light properties.

claim: Light-induced activation of JF-NP-26 in the thalamus caused rapid and robust analgesia in a mouse model of breakthrough cancer pain.
source: For example, light-induced activation of JF-NP-26 in the thalamus caused rapid and robust analgesia in a mouse model of breakthrough cancer pain, a sudden severe, and transient type of pain that may develop in cancer patients under treatment with opioids (Notartomaso et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Notartomaso et al., 2022.

claim: Light-activation of JF-NP-26 can help identify the site within the pain neuraxis where mGlu5 receptor blockade is sufficient to cause analgesia.
source: Light-activation of JF-NP-26 can help identify the site within the pain neuraxis where mGlu5 receptor blockade is sufficient to cause analgesia.
evidence: Logical interpretation of the experimental approach.

claim: Light-inactivation of alloswitch-1 allows to establish the region where mGlu5 receptor blockade is necessary for the induction of analgesia.
source: In contrast, light-inactivation of alloswitch-1 allows to establish the region where mGlu5 receptor blockade is necessary for the induction of analgesia.
evidence: Logical interpretation of the experimental approach.

claim: Prefrontal cortical regions and thalamus are necessary and sufficient for the antinociceptive effects of mGlu5 receptor blockade by systemic NAMs in neuropathic pain conditions.
source: This study shows that prefrontal cortical regions and thalamus are necessary and sufficient for the antinociceptive effects of mGlu5 receptor blockade by systemic NAMs in neuropathic pain conditions.
evidence: Summarizes the main findings of the study.

claim: Local mGlu5 receptor inhibition in the basolateral amygdala produced pronociceptive rather than antinociceptive effects by blocking feedforward inhibition of the central nucleus of amygdala.
source: Unexpectedly, however, local mGlu5 receptor inhibition in the basolateral amygdala produced pronociceptive rather than antinociceptive effects by blocking feedforward inhibition of the central nucleus of amygdala without affecting amygdala output to prelimbic cortex (see Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by behavioral and electrophysiological data, summarized in Figure 4.

claim: Local mGlu5 receptor inhibition in the basolateral amygdala did not affect amygdala output to prelimbic cortex.
source: Unexpectedly, however, local mGlu5 receptor inhibition in the basolateral amygdala produced pronociceptive rather than antinociceptive effects by blocking feedforward inhibition of the central nucleus of amygdala without affecting amygdala output to prelimbic cortex (see Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The use of light-sensitive drugs allowed the demonstration of a heterogenous function of mGlu5 receptors in the pain neuraxis.
source: Thus, the use of light-sensitive drugs allowed the demonstration of a heterogenous function of mGlu5 receptors in the pain neuraxis, which may have important implications for the application of precision medicine in the treatment of chronic pain.
evidence: Summarizes the main conclusion of the study.

claim: The heterogenous function of mGlu5 receptors in the pain neuraxis may have important implications for the application of precision medicine in the treatment of chronic pain.
source: Thus, the use of light-sensitive drugs allowed the demonstration of a heterogenous function of mGlu5 receptors in the pain neuraxis, which may have important implications for the application of precision medicine in the treatment of chronic pain.
evidence: Inferred from the findings showing region-specific effects.

claim: Type-5 metabotropic glutamate (mGlu5) receptors are candidate drug targets for the treatment of neuropathic pain.
source: A large body of evidence suggests that type-5 metabotropic glutamate (mGlu5) receptors are candidate drug targets for the treatment of neuropathic pain.
evidence: Based on established knowledge from the literature.

claim: mGlu5 receptors belong to group-I mGlu receptors and are coupled to Gq/11 proteins.
source: mGlu5 receptors, which belong to group-I mGlu receptors, are coupled to Gq/11 proteins, and their activation leads to polyphosphoinositide (PI) hydrolysis, with the ensuing formation of inositol-1,4,5-trisphosphate and diacylglycerol (Nicoletti et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nicoletti et al., 2011.

claim: Activation of mGlu5 receptors leads to polyphosphoinositide (PI) hydrolysis, with the ensuing formation of inositol-1,4,5-trisphosphate and diacylglycerol.
source: mGlu5 receptors, which belong to group-I mGlu receptors, are coupled to Gq/11 proteins, and their activation leads to polyphosphoinositide (PI) hydrolysis, with the ensuing formation of inositol-1,4,5-trisphosphate and diacylglycerol (Nicoletti et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nicoletti et al., 2011.

claim: mGlu5 receptors are widely expressed in most regions of the pain neuraxis and can contribute to the development of nociceptive sensitization.
source: mGlu5 receptors are widely expressed in most regions of the pain neuraxis and can contribute to the development of nociceptive sensitization.
evidence: Based on established knowledge from the literature.

claim: Pharmacological blockade of mGlu5 receptors has mostly shown antinociceptive activity in preclinical models of inflammatory and neuropathic pain.
source: Pharmacological blockade of mGlu5 receptors has mostly shown antinociceptive activity in preclinical models of inflammatory and neuropathic pain (Mazzitelli et al., 2022; Nicoletti et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mazzitelli et al., 2022 and Nicoletti et al., 2015.

claim: Oral administration of fenobam had minimal temporary analgesic effects and no clinically or statistically significant persistent analgesic effect on heat/capsaicin-induced cutaneous hyperalgesia in healthy volunteers.
source: In contrast, oral administration of a mGlu5 receptor-negative allosteric modulator (NAM, fenobam), had minimal temporary analgesic effects and no clinically or statistically significant persistent analgesic effect on heat/capsaicin-induced cutaneous hyperalgesia in healthy volunteers (Cavallone et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cavallone et al., 2020.

claim: Opposing actions of mGlu5 receptors have been reported in different brain regions.
source: It remains to be determined if, and to what extent, region-specific actions are involved in the analgesic activity of mGlu5 receptor NAMs, considering that opposing actions have been reported (Chung et al., 2018; Kiritoshi et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chung et al., 2018 and Kiritoshi et al., 2016.

claim: Neuropathic pain reflects the development of neuroplasticity that drives nociceptive sensitization in most stations of the pain neuraxis.
source: Neuropathic pain reflects the development of neuroplasticity that drives nociceptive sensitization, i.e., the amplification of pain signal transmission in most stations of the pain neuraxis, including regions of the pain matrix that encode the perceptive and emotional-affective components of pain (Latremoliere and Woolf, 2009; Carozzi et al., 2008; Colloca et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Latremoliere and Woolf, 2009; Carozzi et al., 2008; Colloca et al., 2017.

claim: The drug treatment of neuropathic pain remains a major therapeutic challenge and unmet medical need because of severe side effects and a high percentage of patients resistant to medication.
source: The drug treatment of neuropathic pain, i.e., chronic pain originating from damage or disease of the somatosensory system, remains a major therapeutic challenge and unmet medical need because of severe side effects and a high percentage of patients resistant to medication (Fornasari, 2017; Finnerup et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fornasari, 2017 and Finnerup et al., 2015.
